text: About half the work for this was just passing through the settings via the config, node connector factories, sessions, and connector construct, and updating all tests. The rest was nothing more than a derived connector class. The connector and acceptor are socket factories, establishing one socket connection per instance, managing timeouts, name resolution, bindings, socket config, etc. So this just overrides `connector::handle_connect(...)` and `connector::start(...)` protected base class methods and implements the indirection on the socket strand. <https://github.com/evoskuil/libbitcoin-network/blob/master/src/net/connector_socks.cpp>

elements.text: Once the connection is established the socket is handed off as before with no other impact. Note that the connector operates on the network strand, and establishes sockets - which have their own strand. The socket is used in the handshake with the socks5 proxy server, so that operates on the socket's own strand. Given socket::stop() and all other methods are thread safe and dispatch to its own strand, it's pretty simple. And when already on own strand, dispatch is a no-op. So the communication sequence enters the socket strand and then returns to the connector's network strand, to safely complete the base operations.

I've merged a few updates to the explore interface, which will allow for completion of the block explorer. One of these queries is pretty expensive, since we don't cache fees. Fees require prevouts, and where we skip full validation and client filtering, there's no point at which we have prevout association during sync, which means no fees. The current "block details" query pulls in the whole block and its prevouts in order to compute fee-related values, and a bunch of other stuff available given the populated block.

On a single thread this takes < 100ms for a warm store, which is fine for now. On a cold store the paging cost can bring that up to 1-2 seconds. The cost can be dramatically reduced be de-normalizing the query (not getting the full block/prevouts). We could provide an option to impose fee caching in the exact same way to impose client filter building, which would slightly increase the store size and reduce this query to almost nothing (~3ms, like the others). On the maxi that would raise milestone sync time from 1 hr to 2.5 hrs (basically client filters). Really there's no need for high speed block fee queries, and that would be very reasonable for a server. When performing full validation there would be only trivial time increase.

So a simple approach would be to drop block + prevout computed values into the client filters table and use that as optimized query when available. WRT analogous values for txs, it's probably not work the space to cache such values.

The above is the set of tests against primitive algorithms in wolfssl. For the past couple of days I've been working on the suite of wolfssl unit tests that set up client-server socket communication and perform TLS communication using various protocol variations. There's about 300 of them in the suite of protocols I've set up. Most of this was just getting configuration right, along with a little bit of de-linting. The verbose output is crazy detailed and really shows how complex tls is in all of its variations. So both of these test suites are now integrated into network test. This include their certificates and test driver text files.

boost::asio::ssl::socket compiles cleanly against it, and boost invokes wolfssl context startup and shutdown, using its openssl compat interface, just as a consequence of including <boost/asio/ssl.hpp>. I've also set up a define that can be used to exclude the internal implementation, which would allow the library to be linked against and headers included against openssl, an external wolfssl, or any other compatible library. The internal sources are mostly in their original file layout, and I haven't yet stripped out any unused source files. So the whole library is present, apart from test data and certs that don't get used (old protocols we don't compile). The compile of wolf is entirely isolated from our sources and only takes a few seconds.

I will eventually use the already enabled callbacks to invoke our own hardware optimized sha256, hmac and hkdf, which gives us less code (no redundancy) without the ugly compiler config and raw assembly (which also doesn't work in vc++). The library and its integration with boost give us file system based certificate management.

text: Today I completed the work to open up the network library to external ssl library linkage. So the embedded wolfssl just works with no dependencies, and is picked up automatically by `boost::asio::ssl`. We don't even reference it anywhere in the code.  And dependent libraries pick it up as well. However it can be configured in the `vc++ (visual studio) UI` and via the `install.sh` to exclude the internal linkage, allowing a developer to simply link any `openssl compatible` library (including an external wolfssl). The internal ssl is fully configured and tested, but by linking it externally full control is handed over. This solves the non-trivial problem of making ssl easy as well as flexible.

The socket is now fully able to support `tls` over `tcp` (for electrum/stratum-v1 json-rpc), `http` (bitcoind json-rpc, rest, admin web, rest API), and `websockets` (fully implemented but currently not used).

The remaining work is all connecting the dots between configuration, construction/retention of the ssl context for a given endpoint, and passage of the context via session->acceptor for accept, and acceptor->socket upon tcp connect (at socket construct). Nothing complicated here, so expect to have this all hooked up tomorrow, and be able to start configuring and testing it.

The implementation is able to support packet level privacy, server auth, and client auth, based on context config for a given endpoint, with independent context for each endpoint. It will also support secure and non-secure endpoints for the same service, if enabled by configuration.

Finally, the socket can accept other types of configuration context (variant), and other types of socket streams (also variant), so this will allow drop-in support for zmq::context and p2p::context security. And of course we will need stream types for zmq to implement that framing, as well as for stratum-v2. But now the implementation will allow these to drop right in to config, context, stream, and security.
